questions.question: A fraction bar is cut into 4 equal parts and 2 of the parts are shaded. A second fraction bar of exactly the same length is cut into 8 equal parts. How many of the 8 parts must be shaded so the two bars show equivalent fractions?
options: 4 parts
3 parts, because 8 is 4 more than 4, so shade 1 more part
2 parts, because 2 parts were shaded on the first bar
6 parts, because 8 - 2 = 6
questions.explain: The bars are the same whole, so the same amount must stay shaded: each fourth splits into 2 eighths, so 2/4 = 4/8. The usual trap is keeping the shaded count at 2 and forgetting the denominator changed from 4 to 8.

questions.question: One fraction bar is cut into 3 equal parts with 1 part shaded. A second fraction bar of exactly the same length is cut into 6 equal parts with 2 parts shaded. Which sentence is true?
options: The second bar shows more, because 2 shaded parts is more than 1 shaded part.
They show equivalent fractions, because 1/3 = 2/6.
The second bar shows more, because 6 equal parts is more than 3 equal parts.
The second bar shows more, because a bar cut into 6 parts is a longer bar.
questions.explain: Cutting each third in half turns 1/3 into 2/6, so the same length of bar is coloured: 1/3 = 2/6. The trap is comparing only the shaded counts (2 beats 1) instead of comparing each numerator with its own denominator.

questions.question: A fraction bar is cut into 12 equal parts and 9 of the parts are shaded. Which name describes the very same shaded amount using fewer, larger equal parts?
options: 9, because 9 parts are shaded
questions.explain: Group the 12 parts into 4 groups of 3; the 9 shaded parts fill 3 of those groups, so 9/12 = 3/4. Two common traps: saying just 9 without naming the whole, and naming 1/4, which is the part left unshaded.

questions.question: Ella draws a fraction bar cut into 5 equal parts and shades 3 of them. She wants to draw a second bar that has the same shaded length as her first bar. Which second bar works?
options: A bar the same length as Ella's, cut into 10 equal parts, with 3 parts shaded
A bar the same length as Ella's, cut into 10 equal parts, with 8 parts shaded
A bar twice as long as Ella's, cut into 10 equal parts, with 6 parts shaded
A bar the same length as Ella's, cut into 10 equal parts, with 6 parts shaded
questions.explain: Each fifth splits into 2 tenths, so 3/5 = 6/10 on a bar of the same length. Watch two traps: keeping 3 shaded parts out of 10, and choosing a longer bar, because equivalent fractions must be parts of the same whole.

questions.question: For an art project Emma shades 40 small squares on a 10-by-10 grid of 100 equal squares. Which fraction is equivalent to the part of the grid she shaded?
questions.explain: She shaded 40/100, and dividing the numerator and the denominator by 20 gives 2/5 (4/10 is the same amount too). The trap is answering 40, which counts the shaded squares but never says how many squares make the whole grid.

questions.question: Ravi's family orders a pizza cut into 8 equal slices, and Ravi eats 6 of them. Which fraction of the whole pizza he ate is written with the smallest possible numbers?
questions.explain: He ate 6/8, and dividing both the numerator and the denominator by 2 gives 3/4. Two traps here: 1/4 is the pizza that is left, and shrinking only the denominator gives 6/4, which is more than one whole pizza.

questions.question: On a number line the distance from 0 to 1 is divided into 12 equal steps. A frog sits exactly on the 9th mark after 0. Which fraction names the frog's spot using bigger, fewer steps?
questions.explain: The frog is at 9/12; grouping the 12 steps into 4 groups of 3 shows it sits at 3/4. The trap is changing only one number, like 3/12 or 9/4 — the numerator and the denominator must be divided by the same number, here 3.

questions.question: Noah has a grid with 4 equal columns and 5 rows, so it has 20 small equal squares. He colours 3 whole columns blue. Which statement about his grid is correct?
options: 3 squares are blue, so 3/20 of the grid is blue
3 columns are blue, so the blue part is 3
12 squares are blue, so 12/20 of the grid is blue
15 squares are blue, so 15/20 of the grid is blue, which is the same as 3/4
questions.explain: Each column holds 5 squares, so 3 columns are 3 x 5 = 15 squares, and 15/20 = 3/4 because both numbers divide by 5. The trap is treating each column as one small square and writing 3/20 instead of counting the squares inside the columns.

questions.question: At a birthday party in Surrey there is a large pizza cut into 4 equal slices and a small pizza, exactly half the size of the large one, cut into 8 equal slices. Ben eats 1 slice of the large pizza. Ada eats 2 slices of the small pizza. Ben says: 1/4 = 2/8, so we ate the same amount. Who is right?
options: Ben is wrong: 1/4 = 2/8 only for the same whole, and Ada's pizza is smaller, so Ben ate more.
Ben is right, because 1/4 and 2/8 are equivalent fractions.
Ben is wrong: Ada ate more, because 2 slices is more than 1 slice.
Ben is right, because 4 + 4 = 8 and 1 + 1 = 2.
questions.explain: Equivalent fractions only mean equal amounts when the whole is the same; 2/8 of the small pizza is one quarter of a pizza that is half as big, so Ben's 1/4 of the large pizza is double it. The trap is using 1/4 = 2/8 across two different-sized wholes.

questions.question: Priya's class garden bed is marked into 20 equal squares. On Monday they plant 5 squares with carrots, and on Tuesday they plant 5 more squares with peas. Which statement about the planted part of the bed is true?
options: 10 squares are planted, so the planted part is 10.
1/2 of the bed is planted, because 10/20 = 1/2.
1/4 of the bed is planted, because 5 of the 20 squares were planted each day.
It is the same planted fraction as the neighbour's bed, where 10 of 40 squares are planted, because both beds have 10 planted squares.
questions.explain: First add the two days: 5 + 5 = 10 planted squares out of 20, and dividing both numbers by 10 gives 10/20 = 1/2. Two traps: stopping at 10 without naming the whole, and matching beds just because both have 10 planted squares, since 10/40 is only 1/4.

questions.question: Ms. Chen draws two identical circles on the board. Circle A is cut into 3 equal parts and 2 parts are shaded. Circle B is cut into 6 equal parts. Jordan shades 2 parts of circle B and says both circles show the same amount, because each one has 2 shaded parts. What should Jordan do so circle B really matches circle A?
options: Nothing — 2 shaded parts in each circle already means the same amount.
Shade 3 parts of circle B, because 6 - 3 = 3.
Shade 4 parts of circle B, because every third splits into 2 sixths, so 2/3 = 4/6.
Shade 5 parts of circle B, because 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 + 3 = 6.
questions.explain: Splitting each third into 2 equal pieces turns the 2 shaded thirds into 4 shaded sixths, so 2/3 = 4/6. The trap is matching only the shaded counts — sixths are smaller pieces than thirds, so 2 of them cover far less of the circle.

questions.question: Owen and Mia each get a chocolate bar, and the two bars are exactly the same size. Owen's bar is scored into 10 equal pieces and he eats 4 of them. Mia's bar is scored into 5 equal pieces and she eats 2 of them. Who ate more chocolate?
options: You cannot tell, because a bar in 5 pieces and a bar in 10 pieces are different wholes.
Owen ate more, because 4 pieces is more than 2 pieces.
Mia ate more, because her pieces are bigger than Owen's pieces.
They ate the same amount, because the bars are the same whole and 4/10 = 2/5.
questions.explain: Two of Owen's tenths make one of Mia's fifths, so 4/10 = 2/5 and the same length of bar is gone. The trap is counting pieces instead of fractions: 4 pieces beats 2 pieces only if the pieces are the same size, and here Mia's pieces are twice as big.
